leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Old Medical School
description: Run your eye along the honey-coloured stone of this sprawling Renaissance-style facade and picture the generations of medical students who passed beneath it clutching bags of surgical instruments. For 118 years, until the school moved out to Little France in 2002, this was the beating heart of Edinburgh's medical training, an institution once considered the finest in the English-speaking world. Designed by Sir Rowand Anderson and built between 1876 and 1886, it's forever tied to Joseph Lister, who returned to Edinburgh as Professor of Surgery in 1869 and, working nearby, pioneered the antiseptic techniques that made modern surgery survivable. A plaque by the main entrance still marks his legacy.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: George Heriot's School (Main Building)
description: Golden sandstone, a vast quadrangle, turrets catching the light at every corner — it's easy to see why this place stops people in their tracks. The building's existence traces back to one man's guilty conscience, or perhaps his ambition: George Heriot, royal goldsmith and moneylender to James VI, earned the nickname "Jinglin' Geordie" from the coins rattling in his pockets as he made his rounds of the city. In 1621 he arranged for his fortune to found a hospital and school for fatherless children, though he didn't live to see it — the building was completed and opened as George Heriot's Hospital in 1659. Its imposing Lauriston Place archway, added later by architect William Henry Playfair, remains the grand public face of the school today.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Middle Meadow Walk
address: Middle Meadow Walk, Edinburgh (northern end, near Teviot Place)
description: Feel the avenue open up around you — a broad, tree-lined path running dead straight across open parkland, the kind of quiet green corridor that feels like it shouldn't exist this close to a city centre. It very nearly didn't survive. Laid out by Thomas Hope after 1722 as a raised causeway across a drained loch, over 1,200 trees were later planted along its length, and by 1850 it was marked at either end by ornamental pillars topped with stone unicorns. Since then it has repelled one threat after another: Victorian planners wanted it widened for carriages, and as late as the 1960s the city seriously considered driving a six-lane motorway straight through the Meadows.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Doctors
description: Inside, the Gothic gloom, dark wood and odd medical curios on the walls aren't just decoration — this building has genuinely served the sick and the dead. Built in 1874 to mark the opening of the old Royal Infirmary across the road, it originally housed small trades that fed off the hospital's business: a cabinet-and-coffin maker traded here from 1884 to 1959, and a maker of surgical instruments carried on into the early 1960s. Only after those tenants left did it become a bar, first a short-lived barbecue joint, then a pub called The Mortar from 1970, before finally settling on its current, fitting name, Doctors, in 1979.

name: The Kid's Secret Garden
description: Nothing here quite matches — a hand-painted piano left out in the open, a stegosaurus-shaped tent, mismatched planters and old water pipes repurposed as planters — because nothing here was designed by a council committee. This pocket of the Meadows was created spontaneously in 2016 by local parents and residents who simply decided the space needed to be safer and friendlier for children, and built it themselves, piece by piece, over the years since. It has hosted open-air music, film screenings and community gatherings ever since, entirely on the goodwill of the people who use it. With the Edinburgh Futures Institute now open nearby and Middle Meadow Walk being reshaped, the garden is having to adapt once again to fit its changing surroundings.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Edinburgh Futures Institute
description: Take in the turreted, sandstone bulk in front of you — it looks far more like a Scottish castle than a university building, and that's because it was built to heal, not to teach. Completed in 1879 to designs by architect David Bryce, this was the old Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, its ward pavilions deliberately spaced apart in the fresh air beside the Meadows to reduce the spread of infection, cutting-edge thinking for its time. The hospital served the city until 2003, when it relocated south to Little France. The University bought the site in 2016 and spent seven years and millions of pounds restoring it, reopening the building to the public in June 2024 as a hub for interdisciplinary research, with new public gardens and walkways carved through the old infirmary grounds.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Simpson Loan
description: A quiet residential street of glass and stone now, but the name overhead nods to one of medicine's more reckless breakthroughs. James Young Simpson, an Edinburgh professor of midwifery, spent his evenings testing new chemical compounds on himself and his dinner guests in search of a usable anaesthetic. On the night of 4 November 1847, at his home on Queen Street, he and two colleagues inhaled chloroform before supper and were, in one contemporary's words, "under the mahogany in a trice" — out cold on the floor until morning. Within days he'd announced his discovery to the city's medical society, and chloroform swiftly became the anaesthetic of choice for childbirth, later used by Queen Victoria herself.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Lister Square
description: Pause in this open square, ringed by glass-fronted offices and apartments, and consider that the man it's named for made spaces like this — anywhere with an operating table — dramatically less likely to kill you. Lister Square sits at the heart of Quartermile, the redevelopment of the old Royal Infirmary site, and honours Joseph Lister, the surgeon whose pioneering antiseptic methods slashed post-operative infection rates and made modern surgery survivable worldwide. The wider development takes its own name from its geography: Quartermile is precisely a quarter of a mile, corner to corner, from Edinburgh Castle and the Royal Mile, a neat bit of measuring that turned a working hospital site into a very literal piece of the city's centre.
